clue.text: No spending spree in store!

parts.note: a spree around the shops in which nothing is bought: browsing the displays, looking but never paying

explanation.surface: A shop warns that there will be no big sale on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In store' suggests what a shop has planned, but it means a trip into the shops where you only gaze through the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Gazing at goods in shop displays without buying is a whole excursion where no money is spent.

clue.text: Two capital girls, but 'e's given one the 'slip

indicators.note: the Cockney ''e's given one the 'slip' says one of the two E letters in the first girl's name slips away

parts.note: Winnie is a girl's name
Peg is another girl's name, short for Margaret

explanation.surface: Two girls in the capital give somebody the slip, told in Cockney speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two ... girls' supplies two names, WINNIE and PEG; 'e's given one the 'slip' drops an E from WINNIE, leaving WINNI. The dropped aitches of ''e's' and ''slip' are just Cockney flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnipeg is the capital city of the Canadian province of Manitoba.

clue.text: What title had Mrs. Battle in common with Elia ?

definitions.text: What title had Mrs. Battle in common with Elia ?

parts.words: What title had Mrs. Battle in common with Elia ?
parts.note: Elia was Charles Lamb's assumed name, and one of his essays is about Mrs Battle; the shared title is the French for a war name, and battle suggests war

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question about a character in Charles Lamb's Essays of Elia.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote as 'Elia', a pen name; his essay 'Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist' gives the lady a name that means war, so both carry a 'war name', the French phrase for a pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase literally means a war name and is used for any pseudonym a person adopts.

clue.text: Can be feathered and made to soar

indicators.note: the letters of the next word are made into something else, a rearrangement of them

explanation.surface: Something that can wear feathers is made to soar, like a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Feathering is a rowing term: turning the blade flat as it comes out of the water. 'Made to' signals that SOAR is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowers feather their blades by turning them horizontal between strokes to cut wind resistance.

clue.text: See 1
Good match for the footman ?

parts.note: a female servant whose name pairs a hand with a maid, matching a foot with a man in the male servant's title

explanation.surface: Who would make a suitable bride for the footman in a grand house?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' suggests marriage between servants, but it is also the pairing of names: hand with foot, maid with man.
explanation.definitionFit: A female servant or attendant, historically paired with the male household servant in a great house.

clue.text: Fond hopes of resounding success at the Highland gathering?

definitions.text: Fond hopes of resounding success at the Highland gathering?

parts.words: Fond hopes of resounding success at the Highland gathering?
parts.note: fond hopes are wishful fantasies; at a Highland gathering a resounding success would be what the bagpipers dream of

explanation.surface: Bagpipers at a Scottish games hope their playing will be a triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: A Highland gathering is a Scottish games day with piping contests, so a piper's dream of a loud win puts both words in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanciful hopes unlikely to come true are often called opium-induced fantasies in this idiom.

clue.text: This puts corn up architecturally

parts.note: put these letters after the word corn and you build the moulding along the top of a wall

explanation.surface: A building method that hoists grain up high.
explanation.walkthrough: Added to CORN these three letters make CORNICE, the moulding that crowns a wall; frozen water has nothing to do with the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to the grain word, these letters make the ornamental moulding along the top of a building.

clue.text: It's a let-in for the cloth

definitions.text: It's a let-in for the cloth

parts.words: It's a let-in for the cloth
parts.note: a triangular piece of material let into a garment to widen or strengthen it

explanation.surface: Something that admits members of the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' usually means the clergy, but here it is plain fabric with an extra piece sewn in.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressmaker inserts this triangular or diamond-shaped patch to enlarge or reinforce a seam.

clue.text: Might make a lot, but not on a treble chance

indicators.note: the words a lot might be made into another word by rearranging their letters

explanation.surface: A football pools punter could win a lot, though not on the treble chance.
explanation.walkthrough: The treble chance was a popular British football pools bet. 'Might make' rearranges A LOT; the definition is a voice pitched below treble.
explanation.definitionFit: The low female or high male singing voice lies beneath the treble line, so it is not the treble part.

clue.text: Mule ran wild figuratively

definitions.note: an adverb hinting at a figure, standing for a word that is a figure

indicators.note: running wild means the letters break loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A mule bolted, though the sentence is meant metaphorically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges MULE and RAN. 'Figuratively' normally means metaphorically; here it points to figures, the digits.
explanation.definitionFit: A symbol for a number is a figure, so the definition plays on that sense of figurative.

clue.text: Sleepyheads

parts.note: people who doze, and also heads in slang, so the single word is read as sleepy heads

explanation.surface: People who can't stay awake.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'napper' is a head, so this word for dozers also means heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who take short sleeps doze, and in slang the same word means heads.

clue.text: I have gone right into Bucks for a place

parts.note: I have shortens to I've

explanation.surface: Someone has moved straight into Buckinghamshire to find a home.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks is short for Buckinghamshire, an English county; Iver is a village there, so 'into Bucks' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Iver is a village in south Buckinghamshire, near Pinewood film studios.

clue.text: Epithet for the middling proficient-and altogether doughty

parts.note: taken as written
mid means middle or middling
able means proficient or skilled

explanation.surface: Choosing a description for someone who is only moderately skilled yet bold overall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And altogether' tells you to put the three pieces together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Doughty means valiant and redoubtable, inspiring awe or fear in an opponent.

clue.text: Dancing, love, beside that glorious head of hair — I'm crazy about it

parts.note: ballet is a form of dancing
O is love, a zero score in tennis
a mane is a long, flowing head of hair

explanation.surface: A dancer with flowing hair declares a passion for the art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm crazy about it' speaks for the enthusiast, with 'it' being the dancing in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is passionately devoted to the ballet would say they were mad about it.

clue.text: Sourpuss chaperone for Flora

definitions.note: a collective word for plants, defining a single flower

parts.note: a snap is a short-tempered remark, as from a sourpuss
a dragon is a fierce chaperone

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered chaperone is assigned to a girl named Flora.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora looks like a girl's name for the chaperone to guard, but it means plant life, of which this flower is one.
explanation.definitionFit: This garden flower with blooms like a snapping mouth is one of the plants that make up the plant kingdom.

clue.text: Like one Roman consul and maybe one queen

indicators.note: maybe says the letters given could be put in another order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A comparison with a Roman consul and possibly with a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The emperor Caligula is said to have planned to make his horse Incitatus a consul. 'Maybe' rearranges I and QUEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Of or like a horse; Caligula's favourite horse was reputedly destined for the consulship.

clue.text: Describing the descent of the plumb ?

definitions.text: Describing the descent of the plumb ?

parts.words: Describing the descent of the plumb ?
parts.note: descent can mean ancestry in a direct line, or the fall of the weighted cord a builder uses

explanation.surface: Explaining how a builder's plumb weight drops.
explanation.walkthrough: A plumb line drops straight down, and descent is also family ancestry in a direct line.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes descent in a direct line of ancestry and also refers to a line.

clue.text: Absolute Yorkist incognito

parts.note: Captain Absolute in Sheridan's play The Rivals courts Lydia under a false name, which is also a Yorkshire town

explanation.surface: A thoroughly loyal Yorkshireman travels in disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absolute' looks like an adjective; it is Captain Absolute of Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, who goes by the alias Ensign Beverley. Beverley is a market town in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The disguise name taken by Sheridan's Captain Absolute is also a historic East Yorkshire town.

clue.text: Of great eastern and western engineering fame was one Samuel, poet

definitions.text: Of great eastern and western engineering fame

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A man named Samuel, a poet, was famed for engineering in east and west.
explanation.walkthrough: Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the steamship Great Eastern and the Great Western Railway; 'great eastern and western' reads like ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunel, the Victorian engineer, had this first name and built the Great Eastern and the Great Western.

clue.text: Fine chap, if a bit of a tearaway?

definitions.meaning: in dated slang, a splendid fellow is a ...
literally one who tears or rips things

explanation.surface: A good fellow, even if he is somewhat wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tearaway' means a reckless youth, but here it is read as something that tears things away.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang for a splendid person, and literally a tool or person that tears.

clue.text: These brands are on the way out

definitions.text: These brands are on the way out

parts.words: These brands are on the way out
parts.note: brands are burning pieces of wood, and these are dying down as the fire goes out

explanation.surface: Some commercial brands are falling out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brands' suggests trade names, but a brand is also a piece of burning wood, and these are dying out.
explanation.definitionFit: The glowing remains of a dying fire are burning fragments about to go out.

clue.text: A skeely skipper all of a tremble

definitions.note: the trees' leaves quiver, so they are always trembling

parts.note: Sir Patrick Spens is the skilful sea captain of the Scottish ballad, which asks for a skeely skipper

explanation.surface: A skilled sea captain is shaking all over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skeely' is Scots for skilful; the ballad 'Sir Patrick Spens' asks where to find a skeely skipper. Aspen leaves quiver in the slightest breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees of the poplar family whose leaves flutter constantly, the source of the phrase quaking like a leaf.

clue.text: They're keen, to lead the attack

definitions.text: They're keen, to lead the attack

parts.words: They're keen, to lead the attack
parts.note: sharp points on weapons are keen, and the same word means to lead an assault

explanation.surface: Some eager soldiers volunteer to head the assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like eager but means sharp, as the points of spears are.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp tips of spears are keen, and to head an assault is to be at its front point.

clue.text: Do you go all archaic ?

parts.note: the phrase do you, put into old-fashioned English with thou, uses this verb form

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is lapsing into old-fashioned speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do you' in archaic English becomes 'dost thou', the form here.
explanation.definitionFit: The old second-person singular of the verb do is used with thou in archaic English.

clue.text: The reverse of an open space is an enclosed one

definitions.note: one stands for space, so an enclosed space

indicators.note: the reverse of a word is that word read from its last letter back to its first

parts.note: a moor is an open stretch of uncultivated land

explanation.surface: A paradox: turn an open space round and it becomes closed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reverse of' turns MOOR backwards; 'one' stands for space, so the definition is an enclosed space.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamber inside a building is a walled, enclosed space, the opposite of open land.

clue.text: Water for Mrs. Porter

parts.note: in the old song quoted in Eliot's The Waste Land, Mrs Porter and her daughter wash their feet in a fizzy water

explanation.surface: Fetching water for a woman called Mrs Porter.
explanation.walkthrough: The bawdy song runs: 'The moon shone bright on Mrs Porter / And on her daughter / They wash their feet in soda water', and Eliot quotes it in The Waste Land.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbonated water is what Mrs Porter and her daughter wash their feet in, in the song.

clue.text: Good news

parts.note: the Greek-derived word for the gospel literally means good tidings

explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Greek for good message and refers to the gospel.

clue.text: Frank friend

parts.note: a Frank is a Frenchman, so this is the French word for a pal

explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a pal, French being the language of the Franks.

clue.text: Mouths' the word from picadors to matadors

indicators.note: the letters are taken from within the run of words picadors to matadors

explanation.surface: A word passed from the picadors to the matadors in the bullring.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'picadorS TO MATAdors'. 'Mouths' is a botanical term: the pores in a leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany the breathing pores on leaves are called by the Greek for mouths.

clue.text: Woods awhirl ?

parts.note: small woods, read as if the word were spin plus a fanciful whirling suffix

explanation.surface: Trees spinning round and round.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for small woods begins with SPIN, so it looks as if the woods are in a whirl.
explanation.definitionFit: Small woods or copses are known in Britain by this word.

clue.text: Tip left on the tray

parts.note: a tip suggests money left for a waiter, but here it is the stub of a cigarette in the ashtray

explanation.surface: A gratuity left for a waiter on the tray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' suggests money for a waiter; it is the butt of a cigarette ('fag' is British slang for one) left on the ashtray.
explanation.definitionFit: The stub of a smoked cigarette is its last scrap, typically left in an ashtray.
